report:
Conclusion: the claim “capsaicin treats breast cancer in humans” is **not supported**. The evidence is mainly **preclinical**: breast-cancer cell lines show reduced viability/migration and apoptosis after capsaicin exposure, often via TRPV1 or related pathways, but these are laboratory findings, not patient outcomes (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5167528/). A two-decade systematic review describes heavy research interest and mechanisms, yet does not establish capsaicin as an effective human breast-cancer therapy (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2022.908487/full).

A key caution is translation: reviewers note oral/systemic capsaicin clinical value remains “speculative,” with delivery, exposure duration, and safety problems; animal data even suggest capsaicin-sensitive nerve desensitization can facilitate metastasis in a 4T1 breast-cancer model (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/). In humans, capsaicin’s clearest breast-cancer-adjacent use is **symptom control**, e.g., high-concentration patches for neuropathic pain after breast-cancer surgery—not tumor regression (https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6694/18/14/2355).

Bottom line: capsaicin is biologically active against breast-cancer cells in vitro and remains a research lead, but there is no good clinical evidence that it treats or cures breast cancer in people. Patients should not substitute chili/capsaicin supplements for surgery, endocrine therapy, HER2-targeted therapy, chemotherapy, radiation, or immunotherapy.
